name: Robin Briggs
specialization: Community dynamics of witchcraft accusation; Lorraine regional study

major_works.title: Witches and Neighbors: The Social and Cultural Context of European Witchcraft
major_works.significance: Community-based analysis showing how witchcraft accusations emerged from long-term neighborhood tensions rather than elite persecution

major_works.title: Communities of Belief: Cultural and Social Tension in Early Modern France
major_works.significance: Broader social history framework informing the witchcraft study

core_argument: Witchcraft accusations arose from within communities, not from above. Over decades, a reputation for witchcraft accumulated through neighborhood disputes, charity refusals, and misfortune attribution until a formal accusation became socially possible. The accused witch was typically embedded in the community for years before prosecution, not an outsider scapegoat.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Trial records from the Duchy of Lorraine spanning approximately 1580-1670; community depositions and witness statements
methodological_approach.analysis_target: Social relationships between accusers and accused; patterns of neighborhood tension; long-term reputation formation
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Qualitative case analysis and community network reconstruction from depositions
methodological_approach.explanatory_level: Community-level social dynamics; interpersonal relationships and reputation over time

key_contributions.claim: The typical witch accusation came from a neighbor or community member in long-standing tension with the accused, not from elite or external pressure
key_contributions.implication: Witch-hunting was substantially a community-generated process, not simply top-down persecution

key_contributions.claim: A witch's reputation built over many years of small incidents before formal prosecution; the trial crystallized existing community suspicion
key_contributions.implication: To understand prosecutions, historians must look years or decades before the trial date

key_contributions.claim: Accused persons were not random marginal scapegoats; they were specific individuals with specific histories of conflict with their accusers
key_contributions.implication: Functional explanations (society needs a scapegoat) are insufficient; particular social histories matter

reception_and_critique.major_influences: French social history (Annales school influences), community study methodology, English social history tradition (Thomas, Macfarlane)
criticisms: Lorraine focus may not generalize to regions with different legal or religious structures
Some critics argue insufficient attention to gender as structural factor
The community-dynamics model may underweight the role of demonological ideology in enabling prosecution

historiographical_significance: Briggs produced one of the most detailed and empirically grounded regional studies of witchcraft in European historiography. His demonstration that witch accusations were community-generated rather than elite-imposed challenged both the Murray fertility-cult thesis and simple persecution narratives. His Lorraine database remains a foundational resource.
source_method: Published scholarship and critical historiographical reconstruction
